nameStory: The "netted" in netted shield lichen comes from the distinctive web-like pattern of white lines that crisscross its surface, called pseudocyphellae. These look like tiny cracks or a delicate net has been pressed into the lichen's gray-green surface. The "shield" part refers to its flat, circular growth form that spreads like a protective shield across tree bark.
description: Netted shield lichen is one of New England's most common lichens, forming gray-green circular patches on tree bark that can grow up to 4 inches across. It has a leafy, flat appearance with broadly rounded lobes that overlap like shingles. The distinctive white net-like pattern across its surface makes it one of the easier shield lichens to identify. This tough lichen can handle pollution better than most, so you'll often find it even in urban areas.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive white net-like pattern (pseudocyphellae) that covers the gray-green surface like tiny cracks or veins - this is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, leafy patches with broad, rounded lobes that feel papery and slightly rough to the touch when dry

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Upper surface is pale gray-green to bluish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet; flip it over to see the jet-black underside

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches typically reach 2-4 inches across, though multiple patches often merge to cover larger areas of bark

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always grows on tree bark, especially hardwoods like maples and oaks, but occasionally found on wood fences or rocks

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Produces powdery white or gray soredia along the lobe edges and surface - these feel gritty when rubbed gently with your finger

habitat: You'll find netted shield lichen on the bark of deciduous trees throughout New England, from sea level to mountain elevations. It's particularly common on maples, oaks, and birches in both forests and urban settings like parks and tree-lined streets. This adaptable lichen tolerates pollution well, making it one of the few lichens you can reliably spot in cities and along busy roads.

seasonality.spring: More vibrant green coloration appears as spring rains moisten the lichen, making the white netted pattern stand out dramatically against the darker background.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the lichen appears pale gray and papery, with the network pattern still clearly visible but less contrasted.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture brings out rich colors again, and this is an excellent time to study specimens as deciduous trees shed leaves, exposing more bark.
seasonality.winter: The lichen remains visible year-round on bare deciduous trees, appearing gray and dormant but still showing its diagnostic netted pattern clearly against snow-covered bark.

funFact: This lichen is essentially a living air quality monitor - scientists use it to track pollution levels because it absorbs heavy metals and radioactive particles directly from the air, making it more accurate than some mechanical monitoring devices!
confusionNotes: It's most easily confused with other gray shield lichens, but the white net-like pattern is unique - if you see the "cracked" appearance on the surface, you've got netted shield lichen. Remember: "Netted = white net pattern" for a simple memory trick.
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called "hammered shield lichen" or "cracked-shield lichen" in field guides, referring to the same distinctive surface pattern. Recent DNA studies have revealed that what we call "netted shield lichen" might actually be several very similar species that look identical to the naked eye.
compareHints: Netted shield lichen is distinguished from its shield lichen relatives by its unique white net pattern - bottlebrush shield lichen has tiny finger-like projections, while salted shield lichen has a more uniformly smooth surface with white spots rather than a connected network. The netted pattern is so distinctive that once you've seen it, you won't confuse it with other shield lichens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bottlebrush shield lichen stands out from other Parmelia species by its distinctive branching edge projections - netted shield lichen has a more reticulated (net-like) surface pattern, while salted shield lichen has simpler, less ornate edges.
Unlike its cousin the Netted Shield Lichen which has raised white ridges forming a net pattern, Salted Shield Lichen has scattered granular patches.

Unlike Netted Shield Lichen which has a distinctly white, net-like pattern on its surface, or Bottlebrush Shield Lichen with its fuzzy, hair-like projections, Smoky Crottle has a relatively smooth surface.
Among the shield lichens, fertile shield lichen is distinguished by its pale, prominent pores and frequent fruiting body production.
